name: Budapest
tagline: Imperial grandeur and thermal baths astride the Danube.
whenBlurb: May, June and September are the balm, warm days, thermal baths, café terraces; come August for Sziget or December for the Christmas markets, and avoid the cold, dark heart of winter.

ourTake.lede: Budapest is a thermal-bath city split by the river, and the trick is doing the baths right, go to Széchenyi early morning before the day crowds, or book a private bath session. See the Parliament lit up from the Buda side at night. Skip the ruin-bar tourist crush on weekends; the good ones are quiet on a weeknight.
ourTake.comeIf: You want grand riverside architecture, thermal baths and honest value.
ourTake.skipIf: You want marquee luxury, a coastline or guaranteed sun.

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes, grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

items.name: Four Seasons Hotel Gresham Palace Budapest
items.area: District V / Széchenyi tér, Chain Bridge
credentials: The Leading Hotels of the World
items.description: The city's definitive address, a restored Art Nouveau palace at the Pest foot of the Chain Bridge, looking straight across the Danube to Buda Castle.

items.name: Matild Palace, a Luxury Collection Hotel
items.area: District V / by Elisabeth Bridge, the Danube
items.description: A Belle Époque palace on the Pest riverfront, reborn as a jewel-box hotel, gilded, marbled and unmistakably grand.

items.name: Anantara New York Palace Budapest
credentials: The Leading Hotels of the World
items.description: A history-rich palace hotel wrapped around the legendary New York Café, old-world Habsburg grandeur, restored with a light modern hand.

items.name: The Ritz-Carlton, Budapest
items.description: A dignified 1918 former insurance palace off Erzsébet tér, understated, classical and impeccably run, with a stained-glass cupola over afternoon tea.

items.name: Párisi Udvar Hotel Budapest
credentials: Condé Nast Traveller Readers' Choice Awards 2025
items.description: One of Budapest's most breathtaking interiors, a neo-Gothic-Moorish 1913 arcade with a soaring glass-domed atrium, now a hotel of rare drama.

items.name: W Budapest
items.description: A bold reinvention of the 19th-century Drechsler Palace on Andrássy, opposite the Opera House, design-forward, energetic and beautifully restored.

items.name: Aria Hotel Budapest
items.area: District V / near St. Stephen's Basilica
items.description: A music-themed boutique house steps from the Basilica, crowned by the High Note SkyBar, playful, polished and superbly placed.

items.name: Kozmo Hotel Suites & Spa
items.description: An intimate, contemporary suites hotel with a serious spa, a quieter, design-led alternative to the grand palaces.

items.name: Buda Castle (Budavári Palota)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Budapest, the Banks of the Danube, the Buda Castle Quarter and Andrássy Avenue
items.description: The vast Baroque royal palace crowning Castle Hill, first raised in the 13th century and rebuilt through sieges and centuries, today it holds the Hungarian National Gallery, the Budapest History Museum and the National Széchényi Library. The cobbled courtyards and terraces give a commanding sweep over the Danube and Pest; a private guide turns the layered history into a single unhurried morning for the family.

items.name: Fisherman's Bastion (Halászbástya)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Budapest, the Banks of the Danube, the Buda Castle Quarter and Andrássy Avenue
items.description: A fairytale neo-Romanesque terrace of white stone with seven pointed turrets, one for each of the Magyar tribes that settled the Carpathian Basin in 895, framing the single most photographed panorama in Budapest, straight across to the Parliament. The lower terraces are free; come at first light or dusk to have the arcades and the golden view almost to yourselves.

items.name: Matthias Church (Mátyás-templom)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Budapest, the Banks of the Danube, the Buda Castle Quarter and Andrássy Avenue
items.description: The coronation church of Hungarian kings, its Gothic spire and dazzling diamond-patterned Zsolnay-tiled roof standing at the heart of Castle Hill. Inside, richly painted walls and folk-inspired frescoes make it unlike any church in Europe; the last Habsburg emperor was crowned here in 1916.

items.name: Castle Hill Funicular (Budavári Sikló)
items.description: A charming 1870 wooden cable railway that climbs the steep 48% incline from Clark Ádám Square at the foot of the Chain Bridge to the castle in about 90 seconds. A gentle, characterful way up for grandparents and children who would rather not walk the hill, with a fine view over the river opening as you rise.

items.name: Hungarian Parliament Building (Országház)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Budapest, the Banks of the Danube, the Buda Castle Quarter and Andrássy Avenue
items.description: The riverside icon of Budapest, a soaring neo-Gothic palace of 691 rooms built 1885–1902, its red dome and lace-like spires mirrored in the Danube. Guided tours climb the gilded grand staircase to the Holy Crown of Hungary beneath the central dome; book a timed English tour in advance, as entry is by escorted slot only.

items.name: The Holy Crown of Hungary & Crown Jewels
items.description: The thousand-year-old coronation crown, orb and sceptre, with the famously bent cross atop the crown, displayed beneath the Parliament's central dome as the enduring symbol of Hungarian sovereignty. Seen only on the guided Parliament tour, guarded by ceremonial soldiers; a quietly moving centrepiece of any visit.

items.name: St. Stephen's Basilica (Szent István-bazilika)
items.description: The grandest church in Budapest, its 96-metre dome deliberately matching the Parliament's to equal Buda and Pest in height. Inside, the mummified right hand of St Stephen, the first king, rests in a jewelled reliquary; the panoramic rooftop gallery gives a 360-degree sweep over the whole city. Summer evening organ and orchestral concerts are a lovely, discreet outing.

items.name: Széchenyi Chain Bridge (Széchenyi lánchíd)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Budapest, the Banks of the Danube, the Buda Castle Quarter and Andrássy Avenue
items.description: The first permanent bridge to join Buda and Pest, opened in 1849, its great stone lions and iron chains the emblem of the city. A recently restored evening stroll across, lit up over the black river between the castle and the basilica, is the classic first-night walk, unhurried, romantic and free.

items.name: The Danube Embankments & Promenade
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Budapest, the Banks of the Danube, the Buda Castle Quarter and Andrássy Avenue
items.description: The stretch of quays and terraces on both banks, the Pest side lined with grand hotels and cafés, the Buda side rising to the castle, is the reason UNESCO listed the riverscape itself. A slow evening walk, or a private car pause at a lookout, delivers the bridges and floodlit monuments in one uninterrupted panorama.

items.name: Széchenyi Thermal Bath (Széchenyi Gyógyfürdő)
items.description: Europe's grandest bath complex, a canary-yellow neo-Baroque palace in City Park with 18 pools, the famous steaming outdoor thermal pools where locals play chess in the water, saunas and medicinal springs. The mother of all Budapest baths; book a private cabin and a massage for a serene multi-generational wellness afternoon.

items.name: Gellért Thermal Bath (Gellért Gyógyfürdő)
items.description: The most beautiful of the baths, an Art Nouveau temple of Zsolnay tiles, mosaics and stained glass beside the Danube in the Gellért Hotel. Note: it is closed for a full restoration and is expected to reopen around 2028, so admire the exterior for now and choose Rudas or Széchenyi to bathe.

items.name: Rudas Thermal Bath (Rudas Gyógyfürdő)
items.description: A 16th-century Ottoman bath, an octagonal pool under a domed ceiling pierced with coloured light shafts, paired with a modern rooftop hot tub open to a 360-degree view of the Danube, Parliament and the bridges. The most atmospheric soak in the city, and glorious at night; check the schedule, as the historic Turkish section still keeps single-sex days.

items.name: Lukács Thermal Bath (Lukács Gyógyfürdő)
items.description: The locals' bath, genuinely medicinal springs used since medieval times, its garden walls lined with marble plaques of thanks from cured bathers. Calmer and less touristy than the grand halls, it is the discreet choice for travellers who want the healing waters without the crowds.

items.name: Gellért Hill & the Citadella
items.description: A 235-metre rock rising sheer above the Danube, crowned by the 19th-century Citadella fortress, the finest single viewpoint over the whole city, both bridges and the river bend. A private car can take older travellers most of the way up; sunset here is the classic panoramic reward.

items.name: Liberty Statue (Szabadság-szobor)
items.description: The 14-metre bronze woman holding a palm leaf aloft above the Citadella, visible from across the city, raised in 1947 and long a symbol of the city's freedom. A brief, worthwhile stop woven into the Gellért Hill climb for the view she presides over.

items.name: Cave Church (Sziklatemplom)
items.description: A working Pauline monastery carved into the rock of Gellért Hill, its chapels set inside natural caves opposite the Gellért Baths. An unexpected, hushed and atmospheric detour on the way up or down the hill.

items.name: Great Market Hall (Nagyvásárcsarnok)
items.description: Budapest's grandest indoor market, a soaring 1897 hall of iron and Zsolnay-tiled roof at the Pest end of the Liberty Bridge, stacked with paprika, salami, Tokaji wine and honey below, and food stalls with lángos and paprikás above. A vivid, family-friendly stop for gifts and grazing; the vegetables, cheeses and sweets suit vegetarian palates well.

items.name: Heroes' Square (Hősök tere)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Budapest, the Banks of the Danube, the Buda Castle Quarter and Andrássy Avenue
items.description: The monumental plaza closing Andrássy Avenue, a sweeping colonnade of Hungary's chieftains and kings around the Millennium Monument, flanked by two great art museums. The grandest ceremonial space in the city and an essential photo stop before entering City Park.

items.name: City Park & Vajdahunyad Castle (Városliget)
items.description: Budapest's great green playground behind Heroes' Square, holding a boating lake, the Széchenyi Baths and the storybook Vajdahunyad Castle, a fantasy of Transylvanian Gothic, Romanesque and Baroque built for the 1896 millennium and now the Agricultural Museum. A relaxed, pram-friendly afternoon for all ages.

items.name: Andrássy Avenue (Andrássy út)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Budapest, the Banks of the Danube, the Buda Castle Quarter and Andrássy Avenue
items.description: The elegant tree-lined boulevard running from downtown to Heroes' Square, Budapest's Champs-Élysées, lined with neo-Renaissance mansions, the Opera House and the flagship stores of Gucci, Louis Vuitton and the maisons. A UNESCO-listed avenue best strolled slowly, with a café stop and some discreet luxury shopping.

items.name: Hungarian State Opera House (Magyar Állami Operaház)
items.description: A neo-Renaissance jewel of the 1880s, built to rival Vienna and Paris, gilded and frescoed within and blessed with famously fine acoustics. Take the guided tour of the interiors, or better, attend a performance in one of Europe's most beautiful auditoriums for an unforgettable evening.

items.name: Dohány Street Synagogue (Great Synagogue)
items.description: The largest synagogue in Europe and second largest in the world, a Moorish-Byzantine masterpiece of 1859 with twin onion-domed towers. The complex holds the Hungarian Jewish Museum, the Holocaust memorial garden and the silver weeping-willow Tree of Life, a moving, essential half-day with a guide.

items.name: The Jewish Quarter (District VII)
items.description: The historic Jewish district, now the city's most fashionable quarter, courtyard synagogues, street art, kosher bakeries, designer boutiques and buzzing cafés threaded through handsome old tenements. A rich, walkable afternoon best explored with a private guide who can open its hidden courtyards and history.

items.name: Szimpla Kert (the original ruin bar)
items.description: The mother of Budapest's 'ruin bars', a derelict pre-war building filled with mismatched furniture, fairy lights, art and greenery around an open courtyard. More a cultural landmark than a pub; worth a daytime look at its famous farmers' market and interiors even if late-night crowds aren't your scene.

items.name: House of Terror (Terror Háza)
items.description: A powerful museum in the former secret-police headquarters at Andrássy 60, documenting Hungary's fascist and communist terror and honouring their victims, the very cells where prisoners were held survive in the basement. Sombre and unforgettable; a serious counterweight to the city's grandeur, best for older children and adults.

items.name: Shoes on the Danube Bank
items.description: Sixty pairs of iron shoes cast into the embankment just south of the Parliament, a stark memorial to the Jews shot into the river here in 1944–45, their shoes left on the bank. A brief, deeply affecting pause on the riverside walk.

items.name: Hungarian National Gallery
items.description: The definitive collection of Hungarian art from the Gothic altarpieces to the Impressionist Munkácsy and Csontváry, housed within Buda Castle. The upper-floor terrace and cupola add a fine castle-view bonus; a rewarding indoor morning when the weather turns.

items.name: Museum of Fine Arts (Szépművészeti Múzeum)
items.description: Hungary's finest art museum, on Heroes' Square, with over 100,000 works spanning European masters, El Greco, Raphael, Goya and a superb Egyptian and antiquities collection, reopened after a full restoration. A world-class rainy-day option for art-loving travellers.

items.name: Hospital in the Rock (Sziklakórház)
items.description: A secret WWII and Cold War emergency hospital and nuclear bunker hidden in the caves beneath Castle Hill, preserved with wax figures and original equipment and seen only on a guided tour. A gripping, unusual counterpoint to the palaces above, best for older children and adults.

items.name: Memento Park (Szoborpark)
items.description: An open-air museum on the city's edge where the giant Lenin, Marx and Soviet statues torn from Budapest's squares after 1989 now stand together. A thought-provoking, slightly surreal half-day; a private car makes the out-of-town trip easy.

items.name: Margaret Island (Margitsziget)
items.description: A long green island in the middle of the Danube, car-free gardens, a rose garden, medieval convent ruins, a running track and a musical dancing fountain. The city's favourite retreat for a slow morning; hire a family pedal-carriage or simply walk under the plane trees away from the traffic.

items.name: Danube evening cruise
items.description: The classic way to take in the UNESCO riverscape, the Parliament, castle, bridges and basilica all floodlit gold as you glide past after dark. Charter a private boat with dinner or a glass of Tokaji for a serene, celebratory evening the whole family remembers.

items.name: New York Café
items.description: Long billed as 'the most beautiful café in the world', a riot of gilt, marble columns, frescoed ceilings and chandeliers, once the haunt of Budapest's writers. Reserve for coffee, cake or a grand afternoon tea; go for the astonishing interior as much as the pastries.

items.name: Gül Baba's Tomb & Rose Garden
items.description: The octagonal mausoleum of an Ottoman dervish poet, set in a beautifully restored terraced rose garden high on Rose Hill, the northernmost Islamic pilgrimage site in the world and a place of great calm. A serene, little-visited hideaway with a lovely view over Pest.

items.name: Elisabeth Lookout Tower (Erzsébet-kilátó), Normafa & János Hill
items.description: A neo-Romanesque stone tower atop János Hill, at 527 metres the highest point in Budapest, reached via the scenic Normafa woods and the beloved little Children's Railway or the chairlift. A breezy escape into the green hills with the widest panorama of all; free to climb.

items.name: Bálna (the Whale) & the Danube riverwalk
items.description: A striking glass-and-steel 'whale' of contemporary architecture fusing old brick warehouses on the Pest quay, galleries, cafés and design shops beside the river. A relaxed, modern contrast to the grand old city and a pleasant riverside stop near the Great Market Hall.

items.name: Central Market & artisan food shopping
items.description: Beyond the Great Market Hall, the streets around it hold Budapest's best delicatessens and paprika, foie gras and Tokaji specialists, the place to assemble a hamper of Hungarian gifts. Vegetarian travellers will find superb cheeses, sweet pastries and pickles; a private guide can point you to the finest producers.

items.name: The Danube Bend day trip, Szentendre, Visegrád & Esztergom
items.description: The classic full-day loop north of the city: the cobbled artists' town of Szentendre with its galleries and Orthodox churches, the royal hilltop citadel of Visegrád over a dramatic river curve, and Esztergom with the largest basilica in Central Europe. A private car and guide make it an easy, scenic day for the whole family.

items.name: Szentendre
items.description: A pretty riverside town of pastel houses, artists' studios, Serbian Orthodox churches and marzipan shops, 25 km north of Budapest and reachable in 45 minutes by suburban train. The most relaxed and photogenic half-day escape; charming for a leisurely lunch and a gentle wander.

items.name: Esztergom Basilica
items.description: The largest church in Hungary and one of the tallest in Central Europe, its vast dome rising over the Danube at the Slovak border in the ancient royal city of Esztergom. Climb to the cupola for a sweeping river panorama; a fitting grand finale to the Danube Bend loop.

items.name: Lake Balaton
items.description: Central Europe's largest lake, about 90 minutes from Budapest, the Hungarian 'sea' of vineyards, the Tihany peninsula with its Benedictine abbey and lavender fields, and elegant lakeside villas. A refreshing summer day or an overnight for water, wine and calm; lovely for multi-generational groups.

items.name: Eger & the Valley of the Beautiful Women
items.description: A handsome Baroque town with a famous castle that repelled the Ottomans in 1552, a fine basilica and thermal baths, followed by wine tasting in the cellar-lined Valley of the Beautiful Women, home of the robust 'Bull's Blood' red. A rewarding full day of history, wine and a restorative soak.

items.name: Tokaj wine region
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Tokaj Wine Region Historic Cultural Landscape
items.description: The historic hillside vineyards that gave the world Tokaji Aszú, the golden botrytised dessert wine once 'the wine of kings, the king of wines'. Private cellar tastings among the ancient tunnels reward the longer drive; best combined with an overnight for the full estate experience.

items.name: Vörösmarty Square & the coffeehouse tradition
items.description: The genteel heart of downtown Pest, home to the legendary Café Gerbeaud with its century-old cakes and the Christmas market in winter. A civilised stop for the storied Hungarian coffeehouse ritual, Dobos torte, Eszterházy cake and a slow hour watching the square.

items.name: Fashion Street & luxury shopping (Deák Ferenc utca)
items.description: Budapest's smartest shopping run, a short pedestrian street off Vörösmarty Square lined with international luxury houses, complemented by the maison boutiques along Andrássy Avenue. Discreet, unhurried shopping between sightseeing, with cafés and the grand hotels close at hand.

items.name: Stand
items.description: Szabina Szulló and Tamás Széll's flagship, refined modern Hungarian cooking around a glass-walled kitchen, and the city's most decorated table.

items.name: Babel
items.description: Kornél Kaszás's hushed, elegant room of barely a dozen tables, tasting menus rooted in Austro-Hungarian and Transylvanian tradition, chasing purity of flavour.

items.name: Costes
items.description: The restaurant that won Hungary's first Michelin star in 2010, polished, classical fine dining that set the modern Budapest standard.

items.name: essência
items.description: A love story on a plate, Portuguese chef Tiago Sabarigo and Éva Jenei let you lead each course Portuguese or Hungarian, or weave the two together.

items.name: Rumour by Jenő Rácz
items.description: Jenő Rácz's confident, contemporary tasting menu, technically sharp, produce-led cooking from one of the country's most talked-about chefs.

items.name: Salt
items.description: A single tasting menu built almost entirely on Hungarian produce and craft, foraged, fermented and fiercely seasonal, in the Nordic spirit.

items.name: Borkonyha Winekitchen
items.area: District V / near St. Stephen's Basilica
items.description: 'Wine Kitchen', Ákos Sárközi's relaxed, Hungarian-rooted bistro with a serious, wine-led list, holding its star for over a decade.

items.name: New York Café
items.area: District VII / inside Anantara New York Palace
credentials: Inside a Leading Hotels of the World / MICHELIN One-Key hotel
items.description: Often called the most beautiful café in the world, a gilded, frescoed 1894 palace room of marble columns and Venetian chandeliers.

items.name: Gundel
items.area: District XIV / City Park, by the Zoo
items.description: Hungary's most famous restaurant since 1894, the grand, palatial home of Gundel palacsinta and old-world Magyar ceremony, in the City Park.

items.name: Stand25 Bisztró
items.area: District I / Hold utca market & Várkerület
items.description: The Stand team's casual sibling, hearty, refined Hungarian classics done properly, at a fraction of the flagship's price.

items.name: Goli
items.description: An easygoing modern bistro of small plates and natural wines, inventive, seasonal and squarely the kind of good-value cooking the Bib rewards.

items.name: N28 Wine & Kitchen
items.description: A wine-focused kitchen near the Opera House, considered small plates paired with a deep, characterful list.

items.name: Cabrio
items.description: A natural-wine bar with vintage flair and a leafy terrace, bold, seasonal small plates paired with a 100% natural list.

items.name: 94' Konyha & Bár
items.description: Vibrant, Vietnamese-rooted cooking, fragrant pho and the signature 94' Gohan, bringing real Asian craft to the city.

items.name: Boutiq'Bar
credentials: The World's 50 Best Bars, 50 Best Discovery
items.description: A serious, buzzy cocktail bar just off Andrássy, classics and inventive drinks made with real craft against a bold red interior.

items.name: High Note SkyBar
items.area: District V / Aria Hotel, by St. Stephen's Basilica
credentials: Condé Nast Traveller, among the world's top rooftop bars
items.description: The rooftop of the Aria Hotel, a front-row seat to St. Stephen's Basilica, floodlit and close enough to touch, over polished cocktails.

items.name: 360 Bar
credentials: A landmark Budapest rooftop, on Andrássy Avenue
items.description: A long-running rooftop on Andrássy with a genuine 360-degree panorama of the city, igloo domes in winter, open terrace in summer.

items.name: Szimpla Kert
credentials: Budapest's original and most famous ruin bar (est. 2002)
items.description: The original ruin bar, a derelict apartment block stripped to the brick and filled with fairy lights, salvaged junk, street art and a disused Trabant.

plan.heading: 3 days in Budapest, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip, the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

days.label: Day 1
days.title: The Buda hill and the river

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Settle into Matild Palace, then cross the Chain Bridge and take the funicular up to Buda Castle and the Fisherman's Bastion before the coaches arrive.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Walk the Castle District to Matthias Church, then a quiet lunch and coffee at the terrace of the Hilton overlooking the Danube.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Onyx-successor Salt or, for the classic, the tasting menu at Stand, one of the city's two-star tables.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: A private morning at the Hungarian Parliament, then the Great Synagogue and a walk through the old Jewish Quarter.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Soak and rest at the Széchenyi thermal baths, arranged with a cabin before the afternoon crowds.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Costes Downtown or the wine-led Borkonyha, followed by a nightcap at the Boutiq'Bar.

days.label: Day 3
days.title: Art, market, and the leafy hills

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The Museum of Fine Arts on Heroes' Square, then a stroll down leafy Andrássy Avenue.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The Central Market Hall for paprika and Tokaji, then a drive up to the Buda hills for the view.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A final dinner at Babel or the riverside Spago, ending with pálinka.

items.name: Castle District (Buda)
items.description: Cobbled hilltop streets and river views, quiet and grand.

items.name: District V / Belváros
items.description: The downtown Pest core near Parliament, central and walkable.

items.name: District VI (Terézváros)
items.description: The Andrássy avenue quarter with the opera and cafés, elegant and lively.

events.name: Sziget Festival
events.note: One of Europe's largest music festivals, held on an island in the Danube.

events.name: Budapest Wine Festival
events.note: Hungarian winemakers gather in the Castle District for the harvest-season tasting.

events.name: St Stephen's Day
events.note: The national holiday, marked by a grand fireworks display over the Danube.

onGround.heading: On the ground
onGround.note: Stay in District V (Belváros) or the Castle District for the finest addresses; the thermal baths (Széchenyi, Gellért) reward a discreet early-morning private session before crowds arrive.

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Fly into Budapest Ferenc Liszt International (BUD); a private chauffeur meets you inside the terminal and drives the 30–40 minutes into the city.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: A private driver on standby suits the sprawl between Buda and Pest, though the historic core around the Danube and Castle District is best walked.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: eSIM (Airalo, Yesim) activates on landing; 5G is strong and hotel wifi is reliable throughout the city.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: The Hungarian forint (HUF) rules despite EU membership; cards are accepted almost everywhere, keep light cash, and 10–12% for good service is customary.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: Late spring and early autumn are kind, warm days, cool evenings, the Danube at its best; July-August turns humid and crowded, and January-February is grey and near-freezing.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: No nonstop from India; the clean routing is one stop via Istanbul on Turkish Airlines (strong business cabin) or via a Gulf hub on Emirates/Qatar, roughly 11-13 hours total. Turkish's IST connection is the smoothest for onward Central Europe; use the Turkish Airlines lounge at Istanbul, among the best in the network.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No special vaccinations beyond routine; hepatitis A worth being current on. Tap water is safe to drink. Very safe city; ordinary care against pickpockets in tourist crush and around nightlife.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Easy for vegetarians in central Budapest; Jain is workable if you brief the kitchen (Hungarian cooking leans meat and lard, so specify). Indian food is available, Tandoori Palace and Bombay Express are reliable, and upscale hotels handle veg requests well.
